newsitem.title: USA: Simpson judge moved civil trial along quickly.
newsitem.headline: Simpson judge moved civil trial along quickly.

text.p: Judge Hiroshi Fujisaki set the tone early for O.J. Simpson's wrongful-death case, banning the courtroom camera that helped make his 1995 criminal trial an international spectacle.

The no-nonsense jurist wasted little time in laying down strict ground rules for Simpson's civil trial, which ended on Tuesday with jurors unanimously finding Simpson committed the deadly attacks on his ex-wife Nicole Brown Simpson and her friend Ronald Goldman and ordered him to pay at least $8.5 million.

When, at the beginning of the proceedings, Daniel Petrocelli, the lead lawyer for the plaintiffs, suggested he might take four months to present his evidence, Fujisaki looked at him like a teacher gazing upon a wayward student and said gently, "Weeks, Mr. Petrocelli, weeks."
Unlike Judge Lance Ito in the nationally televised criminal case, Fujisaki allowed few sidebars, held few in-chambers meetings with the attorneys and disposed of lawyers' objections without delay.

During one court session, when Simpson's lead attorney, Robert Baker, continued to argue after Fujisaki had made his decision, the judge told him in a scolding tone, "That's my ruling, counsellor, and you know where you can go with it."

The judge kept civility in the civil trial civil by setting an example to the lawyers. Rarely did he raise his voice -- unlike Ito, who was given to bursts of temper -- and in interrupting the attorneys, Fujisaki would quietly say "Excuse me, excuse me."
When he wanted to get their attention, he would interject with a mild "Helloooo."

Fujisaki also set deadlines and made lawyers stick to them. When the defence asked for an extra day in which to complete their case the judge declined to give it to them, saying "You told me Monday and I'm going to keep you to your word."

The length of the civil trial -- just over four months including a two-week Christmas and New Year holiday break -- was in stark contrast to the drawn-out criminal case, which lasted a year from the start of jury selection.

Fujisaki made it clear from the outset he would not tolerate the circus atmosphere that surrounded the criminal case, with attorneys holding daily press conferences to put their spin on the proceedings.
Soon after being assigned the case he slapped a strict "gag" order on all lawyers, witnesses and parties to the lawsuit, barring them from discussing the trial in public.
Next, saying he did not want history to repeat itself, he banned television and photographers from the courtroom.
In announcing that ruling, Fujisaki said the TV camera in Simpson's criminal trial had "significantly diverted and distracted the participants."
Simpson was acquitted in October 1995 in the murders of his ex-wife and Goldman. In the civil case he faced a wrongful death lawsuit brought by the victims' families.
As a child, Fujisaki, who is Japanese-American, spent time in a U.S. internment camp, like thousands of other U.S. citizens of Japanese descent.

After graduating from law school at the University of California at Los Angeles Fujisaki joined the public defender's office in 1963 and went into private practice in 1970. He later became a municipal court judge and was elevated to the superior court in 1980.
